content: The references provided are a comprehensive list of studies, reviews, and guidelines related to tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, particularly in populations at risk such as individuals living with HIV, children, and healthcare workers. 1. Ferebee SH conducted controlled chemoprophylaxis trials in tuberculosis, providing a general review of the effectiveness of preventive treatments for TB. (Bib Tuberc. 1970;26:28–106). 2. Gao L et al. investigated the incidence of active tuberculosis in individuals with latent TB infection in rural China through a population-based, multicenter, prospective cohort study. The study highlighted the progression risk from latent to active TB. (Lancet Infect Dis. 2017 Oct;17(10):1053–61). 3. Rangaka MX et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the predictive value of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for the development of active TB. This study provided insights into the utility of IGRAs in TB risk stratification. (Lancet Infect Dis. 2012 Jan;12(1):45–55). 4. Mahomed H et al. compared the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) and QuantiFERON-TB Gold® in predicting TB disease in adolescents in South Africa. This cohort study assessed the diagnostic accuracy of these tests. (PLoS ONE. 2011 Mar 29;6(3):e17984). 5. Mathad JS et al. explored the association of quantitative IFN-γ and IL-2 responses with discordance in latent TB test results among HIV-infected pregnant women. This study provided insights into immune responses in co-infected individuals. (Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2016 Jun 15;193(12):1421–8). 6. McCarthy KM et al. reported a high incidence of latent TB infection among South African healthcare workers, emphasizing the urgent need for preventive measures in this high-risk group. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2015 Jun;19(6):647–53). 7. Sharma SK et al. compared TST and IGRA for diagnosing latent TB infection in high TB-burden settings, providing evidence for the relative performance of these diagnostic tools. (PLoS ONE. 2017 Jan 6;12(1):e0169539). 8. Dorman SE et al. evaluated the use of IGRAs and TST for diagnosing latent TB infection in healthcare workers in the United States, highlighting the diagnostic challenges in low TB-burden settings. (Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2013 Dec 3;131203133239003). 9. Zwerling A et al. developed the BCG World Atlas, a database of global BCG vaccination policies and practices, which serves as a resource for understanding the impact of BCG vaccination on TB diagnostics. (PLoS Med. 2011 Mar 22;8(3):e1001012). 10. Zunza M et al. reviewed the use of isoniazid for preventing TB in HIV-infected children, providing evidence for its safety and efficacy in this vulnerable population. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. pub3 67). 11. Smieja M et al. reviewed the use of isoniazid for preventing TB in non-HIV-infected individuals, summarizing its role in TB prophylaxis. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. CD001363). 12. Zennar D et al. conducted a network meta-analysis to update the treatment options for latent TB infection, comparing various regimens for efficacy and safety. (Ann Intern Med. 2017 Aug 15;167(4):248). 13. Comstock GW examined the optimal dosage of isoniazid required for TB prevention in immunocompetent adults, providing guidance on effective prophylactic regimens. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 1999 Oct;3(10):847–50). 14. Den Boon S et al. reviewed the continuous use of isoniazid for treating latent TB infection in people living with HIV, emphasizing its role in reducing TB incidence in this population. (AIDS. 2016 Mar;30(5):797–801). 15. Stagg HR et al. performed a network meta-analysis to evaluate treatment options for latent TB infection, providing a comparative analysis of different regimens. (Ann Intern Med. 2014 Sep 16;161(6):419). 16. Galli L et al. analyzed pediatric TB cases in Italy, presenting epidemiological and clinical data from the Italian Register of Pediatric Tuberculosis. (IJMS. 2016 Jun 17;17(6):960). 17. Spyridis NP et al. compared the effectiveness of a 9-month isoniazid regimen versus shorter regimens combining isoniazid and rifampin for treating latent TB infection in children. (Clin Infect Dis. 2007 Sep 15;45(6):715–22). 18. Van Zyl S et al. studied adherence to anti-TB chemoprophylaxis and treatment in children, highlighting challenges in ensuring treatment completion. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2006 Jan;10(1):13–8). 19. Menzies D et al. compared 4 months of rifampin therapy to 9 months of isoniazid therapy for latent TB infection in adults, focusing on treatment completion and adverse events. (N Engl J Med. 2018 Aug 2;379(5):440–53). 20. Diallo T et al. assessed the safety and side effects of rifampin versus isoniazid in children, providing evidence for the tolerability of these regimens. (N Engl J Med. 2018 Aug 2;379(5):454–63). 21. Swindells S et al. evaluated a 1-month regimen of rifapentine plus isoniazid for preventing HIV-related TB, demonstrating its efficacy and safety. (N Engl J Med. 2019 Mar 14;380(11):1001–11). 22. Sterling TR et al. studied a 3-month weekly regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for treating latent TB infection in HIV-co-infected individuals, showing its effectiveness. (AIDS. 2016 Jun;30(10):1607–15). 23. Villarino ME et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial to evaluate a 3-month, 12-dose regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for preventing TB in children and adolescents. (JAMA Pediatr. 2015 Mar 1;169(3):247). 24. Moro RN et al. examined the safety of latent TB treatment during pregnancy, providing insights into the management of TB in pregnant women. (Ann Am Thorac Soc. 2018 May;15(5):570–80). 25. Belknap R et al. compared self-administered versus directly observed therapy for once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine treatment of latent TB infection, highlighting the feasibility of self-administration. (Ann Intern Med. 2017 Nov 21;167(10):689). 26. Podany AT et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of efavirenz in HIV-infected individuals receiving rifapentine and isoniazid for TB prevention, addressing drug-drug interactions. (Clin Infect Dis. 2015 Oct 15;61(8):1322–7). 27. Weiner M et al. investigated the pharmacokinetic interaction of rifapentine and raltegravir in healthy volunteers, providing data on potential drug interactions. (J Antimicrob Chemother. 2014 Apr 1;69(4):1079–85). 28. Brooks KM et al. reported cytokine-mediated systemic adverse drug reactions in a study of dolutegravir with once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine, emphasizing the need for monitoring. (Clin Infect Dis. 2018 Jul 2;67(2):193–201). 29. Dooley KE et al. evaluated the safety and pharmacokinetics of weekly rifapentine/isoniazid in adults with HIV on dolutegravir, providing evidence for its use in this population. (Abstract presented at TB: From Contact to Cure and Beyond, Seattle, WA, USA; 2019). 30. Gupta A et al. conducted a randomized trial on the safety of isoniazid preventive therapy during or after pregnancy, addressing critical issues in maternal and pediatric HIV care. (Abstract presented at Critical Issues in Women’s Health and Early Treatment of Pediatric HIV Infection, Boston, MA, USA; 2018). 31. Taylor AW et al. studied pregnancy outcomes in HIV-infected women receiving long-term isoniazid prophylaxis for TB and antiretroviral therapy, providing data on maternal and fetal safety. (Infect Dis Obstet Gynecol. 2013;2013:1–5). 32. Salazar-Austin N et al. examined the impact of isoniazid preventive therapy on pregnancy outcomes in HIV-infected women in the Tshepiso cohort, highlighting its safety profile. (Clin Infect Dis. 2019 Oct 21;ci1024). 33. Kalk EK et al. reviewed the safety and effectiveness of isoniazid preventive therapy in HIV-infected pregnant women on ART in routine care, emphasizing its programmatic implications. (Reprod Toxicol. 2018 Sep;80:155). 34. WHO guidelines for the treatment of drug-susceptible TB and patient care were updated in 2017, providing comprehensive recommendations for TB management. (Geneva, WHO; 2017). 35. Takizawa T et al. studied the comparative arthropathy of fluoroquinolones in dogs, providing insights into potential adverse effects of these antibiotics. (Hum Exp Toxicol. 1999 Jun;18(6):392–9). 36. Hampel B et al. reviewed the worldwide clinical experience of ciprofloxacin in pediatrics, focusing on safety data from compassionate use. (Pediatr Infect Dis J. 1997 Jan;16(1):127–9). 37. Warren RW discussed the rheumatologic aspects of pediatric cystic fibrosis patients treated with fluoroquinolones, addressing potential adverse effects. (Pediatr Infect Dis J. 1997 Jan;16(1):118–22). 38. WHO consolidated guidelines on TB preventive treatment were updated, incorporating changes to recommendations for latent TB infection testing and treatment. (Geneva, WHO; 2018). 39. Acar S et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on pregnancy outcomes following quinolone and fluoroquinolone exposure, providing evidence for their safety profile. (Reprod Toxicol. 2019 Apr;85:65–74). 40. The FDA issued a safety announcement reinforcing information about serious low blood sugar levels and mental health side effects associated with fluoroquinolone antibiotics, requiring label changes. (FDA, 2018). 41. The European Medicines Agency restricted the use of quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics due to disabling and potentially permanent side effects. (EMA, 2019). 42. WHO developed a mobile app to support the programmatic management of latent TB infection, advancing global TB care. (WHO, 2017). 43. Getahun H et al. emphasized the need for advancing global programmatic management of latent TB infection in at-risk populations, providing a framework for implementation. (Eur Respir J. 2016 May;47(5):1327–30). 44. Sotgiu G et al. reviewed monitoring toxicity in individuals receiving treatment for latent TB infection, comparing systematic reviews with expert opinions. (Eur Respir J. 2015 Apr;45(4):1170–3). 45. Balcells ME et al. examined the risk of resistant TB associated with isoniazid preventive therapy, providing evidence for its safety in preventing resistance. (Emerg Infect Dis. 2006 May;12(5):744–51). 46. Den Boon S et al. reviewed rifampicin resistance after treatment for latent TB infection, providing a systematic analysis of resistance development. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2016;20(8):1065–71). 47. The WHO companion handbook to guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant TB provides detailed recommendations for managing resistant TB cases. (Geneva, WHO; 2015). 48. WHO guidelines on active TB drug-safety monitoring and management (aDSM) were developed to ensure the safe use of TB medications. (Geneva, WHO; 2015). 49. WHO supplementary updates to TB preventive treatment recommendations incorporated changes to improve clarity and implementation. (Geneva, WHO; 2018). These studies and guidelines collectively provide a robust foundation for understanding and managing TB, particularly in high-risk populations, and emphasize the importance of preventive strategies, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment safety.
